tasks.name: Length-Generalizing Counting Encoder
tasks.summary: Studies how sequence encoders maintain integer counters across in-distribution and length-out-of-distribution inputs.
tasks.description_md:
# Synth-Counting

## Research Question
Can you design a sequence-model architecture that maintains *integer counters*
robustly across in-distribution **and** length-out-of-distribution test inputs?
The component under study is the **encoder architecture** (recurrent /
transformer / state-space / hybrid) — initialization, optimizer, training loop,
loss, evaluation, and data generators are fixed.

## Background
Counting is one of the oldest probes of sequence-model expressivity. Weiss,
Goldberg & Yahav (ACL 2018, arXiv:1805.04908) showed that finite-precision
LSTMs can learn to implement integer counters and extrapolate to inputs longer
than those seen at training time, while Bhattamishra, Ahuja & Goyal
(EMNLP 2020, arXiv:2009.11264) demonstrated that vanilla Transformers with
sinusoidal positional encodings collapse on counter languages such as
a^n b^n c^n when the test length leaves the training range. More recent work —
notably McLeish et al. ("Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right
Embeddings", NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2405.17399, repo
https://github.com/mcleish7/arithmetic) — has shown that with the *right
positional embeddings* (Abacus PE indexing offsets within a contiguous numeric
block) Transformers can extrapolate 6x in length on counting-style tasks.

## Fixed Setup

| Label        | Task                                          | Train length     | OOD length          |
|--------------|-----------------------------------------------|------------------|---------------------|
| `exact`      | Regress `y = #(a in x)` over `{a, b}^T`       | `T in [8, 64]`   | `T in [128, 256]` (score = OOD accuracy) |
| `abc`        | Binary classify `a^n b^n c^n` vs corruptions  | `3n in [3, 63]`  | logged on `n in [22, 85]`; score = in-dist accuracy |
| `length-ood` | Same generator as `abc`, but the score is the **retention** `1 - max(0, in_dist_acc - ood_acc)` on `n in (T/3, 4T/3]` | `3n in [3, 63]`  | `n in [22, 85]`     |

Each environment uses the same fixed training loop (6,000 steps of AdamW,
batch 64, smooth-L1 for regression / BCE-with-logits for classification) and
evaluates on 1,024 freshly drawn examples per split. All data is generated on
the fly — no network or filesystem access required.

## What You Can Modify
Edit only the body of `build_model(config: TaskConfig) -> nn.Module` in
`pytorch-examples/synth_counting/custom_strategy.py` (the EDITABLE block
labelled in the file). The returned module must satisfy:

* **Input**: `tokens` `LongTensor[B, T]` padded with `config.pad_id`; the first
  position is always a CLS token. `lengths` `LongTensor[B]` gives the true
  length **including** the CLS token.
* **Output**: a tensor of shape `[B, config.hidden_dim]` representing the
  pooled sequence summary. The fixed head turns that into a scalar.
* **Capacity**: at most 5,000,000 parameters (asserted at startup).

You may freely change the encoder type (RNN, Transformer, SSM, …), positional
embedding scheme, number of layers, attention pattern, etc. The interface
contract is the only hard constraint.

## Metrics
For every environment the script prints `FINAL_METRICS` and `TEST_METRICS`
lines containing `in_dist_accuracy`, `ood_accuracy`, `extrapolation_gap`, and
the primary `score` (already in `[0, 1]`). The aggregate task score is the
geometric mean across the three environments.

## Baselines

| Baseline      | Architecture                                                                                                                                                          | Notes / Reference                                                                                                       |
|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `lstm`        | 2-layer LSTM reading the last hidden state                                                                                                                            | Weiss/Goldberg/Yahav 2018 counter recipe (arXiv:1805.04908). Strong counter baseline.                                   |
| `transformer` | 2-layer Transformer encoder, 4 heads, sinusoidal PE, CLS pooling                                                                                                      | Bhattamishra et al. 2020 vanilla baseline (arXiv:2009.11264). Known to fail length-OOD.                                  |
| `abacus`      | 2-layer Transformer with **Abacus-style count-positional embeddings** (1-based offset within current run-length, with random training offsets, added to token embedding) — current SOTA for counting-style length generalization. | McLeish et al. 2024 (arXiv:2405.17399, repo https://github.com/mcleish7/arithmetic).                                     |

Expected ordering: `abacus` >= `lstm` >> `transformer` (especially on
`length-ood`), matching the literature partial ordering for counting tasks
with length extrapolation.

## Hints
* Counting is fundamentally a recurrence problem. Architectures with an
  explicit memory of "how many" tend to dominate (Weiss et al. 2018).
* Position encodings that depend on **absolute** sequence index rarely
  extrapolate; encodings that depend on a **task-relevant counter** (Abacus,
  position coupling, relative offsets within a block, …) tend to.
* Aggressively shrinking the architecture (low `nhead`, low width) often
  helps Transformers on counter tasks because the model has to commit to a
  single counting attention head rather than memorising shortcuts.

tasks.name: Deep Matrix Factorization Recovery
tasks.summary: Studies how matrix-factorization parameterizations and optimizers recover low-rank matrices from sparse observations.
tasks.description_md:
# Synthetic Matrix Completion: Neural Matrix Factorization Architecture

## Research Question
Given a sparse subset of entries of an unknown rank-r ground-truth matrix M*,
how should we **parameterize a neural matrix factorization** (depth, initialization,
regularization, optimizer) so that gradient descent recovers M* as accurately
as possible on the *unobserved* entries?

This is the canonical "deep matrix factorization" question studied by Arora,
Cohen, Hu, Luo, "Implicit Regularization in Deep Matrix Factorization"
(NeurIPS 2019; [arXiv:1905.13655](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.13655)). They
showed empirically that *increasing the depth* of the factorization
M = W_d W_{d-1} ... W_1 introduces a stronger implicit bias toward low-rank
solutions, often beating both shallow factorizations and classical
nuclear-norm minimization.

## Background
Low-rank matrix completion is fundamental in collaborative filtering, signal
processing, and statistics. Classical approaches solve a convex relaxation
(minimize nuclear norm subject to fitting the observations) via algorithms
like SVT ([Cai-Candes-Shen 2010](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.3286)) or perform
explicit non-convex factorization via alternating minimization
([Jain-Netrapalli-Sanghavi 2012](https://arxiv.org/abs/1212.0467)).

Deep matrix factorization replaces the explicit rank constraint with depth:
write M as a product of d square (full hidden dim) bias-free linear layers
and minimize the squared error on observed entries by gradient descent. With
small initialization the resulting solution biases towards low effective
rank, and depth d >= 3 makes this bias sharper than depth 2 (and stronger
than the implicit nuclear-norm regularizer at low observation rates).

## What You Can Modify
Edit the scaffold file `pytorch-examples/synth_matrix_completion/custom_strategy.py`
inside the EDITABLE block. Concretely, the editable region contains:

1. `build_strategy() -> MatrixRecoveryStrategy` — the entry point the driver calls.
2. The `MatrixRecoveryStrategy` interface declaration.
3. One or more reference strategy classes (default: `DeepMatrixFactorization`).

You may completely replace the strategy class with any algorithm you like
(deeper factorizations, alternative initializations, balanced
parameterization, IRLS, ADMM, SVT, AltMin, neural ODE inits, etc.) as long
as the returned object implements `recover(observed_values, observed_mask,
n, rank_hint, device, max_iters, log_iters) -> torch.Tensor` of shape
`[n, n]`.

## Fixed Setup
- **Ground truth**: random rank-r matrix M* = (U V^T) / sqrt(r) with
  U, V ~ N(0, 1) i.i.d. of shape `[n, r]`, rescaled to `||M*||_F = n`.
  (Same construction as Arora et al. 2019; `gen_gt.py` in their repo.)
- **Observations**: uniformly random subset of the n*n entries at the
  configured observation rate (`gen_obs.py` in the reference repo).
- **Driver**: in the release configuration, samples one matrix and runs
  one initialization per top-level seed, then calls `strategy.recover(...)`
  with a hard iteration budget.
- **Metric**: relative Frobenius error on the *unobserved* entries
  (`test_rel_fro = ||(estimate - M*)[~mask]||_F / ||M*[~mask]||_F`), where
  lower is better. A derived `score = max(0, 1 - test_rel_fro)` may be printed
  for feedback, but the benchmark score spec uses `test_rel_fro` directly.
- Compute budget: each test command must finish in under 30 minutes on a
  single H100.

## Interface Notes
- `recover(...)` receives `observed_values` (M* masked to zero off the
  observation set), `observed_mask` (bool [n, n]), `n`, `rank_hint`
  (the true rank — you may use or ignore), `device`, `max_iters`, and
  `log_iters`.
- Return a CPU or GPU `torch.Tensor` of shape `[n, n]`. The driver moves
  it to CPU and casts to float32.
- Please emit `TRAIN_METRICS iter=... train_mse=...` periodically so the
  agent loop sees training progress.

## Fixed Setup
Three configurations are evaluated:
- `rank3-50`: n=50, rank=3, 30% observed.
- `rank5-100`: n=100, rank=5, 20% observed (the canonical Arora setup).
- `rank10-200`: n=200, rank=10, 10% observed (harder, larger-scale).

The leaderboard primary metric per environment is `test_rel_fro` (lower better).
The task-level score is the geometric mean of normalized `test_rel_fro` terms
across the three environments.

## Baselines
- **shallow_mf** — Depth-2 matrix factorization (`M = W_2 W_1`),
  Gaussian init scale `1e-3`, Adam. Mirrors the depth-2 curve of Arora
  et al. (2019), Figure 1.
- **nuclear_norm** — Singular Value Thresholding ([SVT, Cai-Candes-Shen
  2010, arXiv:0810.3286](https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.3286)) with `tau = 5n`
  and step size `delta = 1.2 / observation_rate`. Classical convex
  baseline.
- **deep_mf** — *SOTA*: Depth-3 deep matrix factorization with small
  Gaussian init (`init_scale = 1e-3`) and learning rate `1e-3`, Adam. The
  depth-3 curve in
  Arora et al. (2019), Figure 1, which "significantly outperforms depth 2"
  at low observation counts and beats nuclear norm (Figure 2).

## Hints
- Empirically, very small init magnitudes (~1e-3 to 1e-6) are essential
  for the depth-induced implicit regularization to kick in (Arora 2019).
- The driver hands you the **true rank** as `rank_hint`. You may rely on
  it if your method needs a rank input (e.g. for AltMin or SVT
  thresholding), or design a rank-agnostic recovery.
- Going deeper than 3 (k=4, k=5) does not necessarily help further: in
  Arora et al. (2019, Figure 2 caption) "results for depth 4 were
  indistinguishable from those of depth 3".
- Watch the train_mse: deep MF at very small init can take thousands of
  steps before train_mse drops sharply — the same kind of "hidden
  progress" / phase transition seen in other implicit-regularization
  experiments. Budget your `max_iters` accordingly.

tasks.name: Differentiable DNF Learner
tasks.summary: Studies how neural learners and training recipes recover random DNF concepts from uniformly sampled examples.
tasks.description_md:
# Synth-DNF

## Research Question
What differentiable neural architecture and training recipe should you choose to learn
**DNF concepts** (disjunctive normal form Boolean functions) from random
uniform examples?

Formally, a DNF over `n` Boolean variables `x ∈ {0,1}^n` is a function
`f(x) = T_1(x) ∨ T_2(x) ∨ ... ∨ T_s(x)`, where each term `T_l` is a
conjunction (AND) of literals `x_i` or `¬x_i`. The agent is given
uniformly drawn training pairs `(x, f(x))` from a *hidden* random target
DNF and must train a classifier that predicts `f` on a fresh test sample.

## Background
DNF learnability under the uniform distribution is one of the most
studied problems in computational learning theory.

* **Quasi-polynomial bound (Verbeurgt 1990):** any `s`-term DNF can be
  learned in `n^{O(log s/ε)}` time under the uniform distribution from
  random examples — but the dependence on `s` is super-polynomial.
* **Membership-query SOTA (Jackson 1997, Harmonic Sieve):** polynomial
  time, but **requires membership queries** so it is not a "neural
  learner from random samples" baseline.
* **Random-DNF average case (Jackson & Servedio, 2005):** polynomial-time
  algorithms exist for random monotone DNF with `s = O(n^{2-γ})` terms
  and random non-monotone DNF with `s = O(n^{3/2-γ})` terms,
  http://www.cs.columbia.edu/~rocco/papers/random05.html.

On the empirical side, vanilla MLPs and gradient-boosted trees are the
canonical practical baselines on Boolean tabular data; recent
"differentiable DNF" architectures (Payani & Fekri 2019, Mat_DNF 2023)
encode the DNF inductive bias directly into the network.

This task asks: *with random examples only, can you design a differentiable
neural learner that closes (or beats) the gap to GBDTs on the three DNF
regimes below*?

## What You Can Modify
Edit only the EDITABLE region (build_model / make_dataset /
fit_and_predict) of
`pytorch-examples/synth_dnf/custom_strategy.py`. Everything else,
including DNF sampling, test-set construction, and final scoring, is
fixed.

This is a neural-learner ML-science task, not a SAT solver or
membership-query algorithm task. Treat the target DNF as a hidden label
oracle for uniformly sampled examples only; do not inspect or reconstruct
the term list directly.

The three signatures you control:

1. `build_model(config, seed) -> (model, info)` returns an opaque model
   object consumed only by your own `fit_and_predict`.
2. `make_dataset(dnf, config, seed) -> (x, y)` constructs the training
   set. Must use only the API exposed via `evaluate_dnf` /
   `make_uniform_examples`, return inputs in `{0,1}^n` and labels in
   `{0,1}`, and stay within `4 * config.train_size` examples.
3. `fit_and_predict(model, info, train_x, train_y, test_x, config, seed)
   -> predictions` does the actual training and returns an integer 0/1
   prediction vector of length `test_x.shape[0]`.

Available imports include `numpy`, `torch`, standard `sklearn` baselines,
and the helpers `evaluate_dnf`, `make_uniform_examples`.

## Fixed Setup
Three families of random DNF targets are evaluated independently and
combined via geometric mean:

| label                    | n  | s  | w | family               |
|--------------------------|----|----|---|----------------------|
| `random-n30-s10-w4`      | 30 | 10 | 4 | mixed-polarity DNF   |
| `monotone-n40-s20-w4`    | 40 | 20 | 4 | monotone DNF         |
| `sparse-n60-s10-w4`      | 60 | 10 | 4 | 12-variable junta    |

For each environment in the release configuration, one hidden target DNF
is sampled per top-level seed. The learner is fit on one fresh training
set and evaluated on a 10k held-out uniform sample. The reported
`test_accuracy` is that run's held-out accuracy.

## Metric
The leaderboard metric is `test_accuracy` (also emitted as `score`) per
environment, then aggregated by geometric mean across environments.

## Baselines
* **mlp** — 2-hidden-layer ReLU MLP (256, 256) trained with AdamW + BCE
  (the canonical neural baseline; vanilla feed-forward networks have no
  DNF-specific inductive bias).
* **rf** — sklearn `RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200)`, the
  classical bagging-of-trees baseline (Breiman, 2001).
* **gbdt** — sklearn `GradientBoostingClassifier`, the strong
  practical baseline for tabular Boolean data (Shwartz-Ziv & Armon,
  arXiv:2106.03253).
* **deep_dnf** — *SOTA neural baseline.* A differentiable DNF
  architecture with `2s` soft conjunctions and a noisy-OR aggregator,
  trained with literal-sparsity regularisation. Follows the
  "differentiable DNF" family (Payani & Fekri 2019, arXiv:1904.01554;
  Mat_DNF, Machine Learning 2023).

## Hints
* The random-DNF base rate is *not* 0.5: with `s` terms of width `w`,
  the probability that a uniform example satisfies at least one term is
  roughly `1 - (1 - 2^{-w})^s`, so for `s=10, w=4` it is about
  `47%` — the majority-class baseline is already near 0.53.
* On the **sparse** environment, identifying the 12 influential
  variables is the entire game; ordinary trees do this naturally.
* DNFs are unions of *axis-parallel* sub-cubes — tree-based learners
  capture this structure for free, while MLPs typically need either
  parity-style features or explicit DNF-shaped inductive bias.

tasks.name: Length-Generalizing Copy Positional Encoding
tasks.summary: Studies how positional and attention mechanisms let small causal Transformers solve copy, repeat, and reverse tasks beyond training lengths.
tasks.description_md:
# synth-copy

## Research Question
What positional / attention mechanism best lets a small causal Transformer
solve algorithmic copy-style tasks at sequence lengths longer than those
seen during training?

## Background
Sequence copy / repeat / reverse are textbook synthetic tasks for studying
algorithmic generalisation in neural sequence models. With recurrence (LSTM)
they are easy at training length but the model is forced to compress every
input character through a fixed-size hidden state; with self-attention they
become trivially solvable at the *training* length but their behaviour at
unseen, longer lengths is dominated by the choice of **positional encoding**.

Kazemnejad, Padhi, Natesan Ramamurthy, Das, and Reddy (NeurIPS 2023,
"The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers",
arXiv:2305.19466) trained 12-layer decoder-only Transformers on content of
length L = 20 and evaluated up to 2L = 40 across Copy and Reverse (their
"primitive tasks"). They find a strong qualitative ordering when going from
in-distribution to length OOD: **NoPE (no positional encoding) > T5 relative
bias > ALiBi > Rotary > sinusoidal/learned absolute**. Press, Smith, and
Lewis (ICLR 2022, "Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases",
arXiv:2108.12409) introduced ALiBi specifically to make Transformers
extrapolate length without retraining. Vaswani et al. (NeurIPS 2017,
"Attention Is All You Need", arXiv:1706.03762, §3.5) introduced the
sinusoidal scheme that still serves as the canonical baseline. Bahdanau,
Cho, and Bengio (ICLR 2015, "Neural Machine Translation by Jointly
Learning to Align and Translate", arXiv:1409.0473) established the
recurrent attention seq2seq baseline used here as a non-Transformer
reference.

## What You Can Modify
Edit the scaffold file `pytorch-examples/synth_copy/custom_strategy.py`
only inside the editable block containing:

1. `build_positional_scheme(config) -> PositionalScheme`
2. `build_model(config) -> nn.Module`

A `PositionalScheme` is a thin container with three optional hooks:
- `token_embedding_extra(positions)` — additive token-level embedding
  (e.g. sinusoidal / learned APE);
- `attn_bias(T, device, dtype)` — additive `[n_heads, T, T]` (or
  `[1, T, T]`) attention-score bias (e.g. ALiBi, T5 relative bias);
- `rotary(q, k)` — applied inside attention before the dot product
  (e.g. RoPE).

Any learnable parameters must be registered via
`scheme.extra_modules` (an `nn.ModuleList`) so that AdamW picks them up.
You may also swap the backbone in `build_model` (e.g. by passing
`use_lstm=True` to `SeqModel`).

## Fixed Setup
- Vocabulary: 16 symbols plus PAD / BOS / EOS / SEP (vocab_size = 20).
- Sequence layout: `[BOS] x_1 ... x_T [SEP] y_1 ... y_M [EOS]`.
  Loss is computed only on positions whose next-token belongs to the target.
- Variants (one test command each):
  - `delim`: y = x (copy after a delimiter).
  - `repeat`: y = x repeated `repeat_k = 2` times.
  - `reverse`: y = reverse(x).
- Train content lengths are sampled uniformly from `[1, L_train=20]`.
- Evaluation: greedy decoding on two splits per variant:
  - `id`: lengths from `[1, L_train]`;
  - `ood`: lengths from `[L_train+1, 2 L_train]`.
- Model: 4 layers, `d_model = 128`, 4 heads, GELU MLP with 4x expansion.
- Optimization: AdamW, lr = 5e-4, wd = 1e-2, batch 256, 6,000 steps,
  200-step linear warm-up, grad-clip 1.0.

## Interface Notes
- `build_positional_scheme(config)` must return a `PositionalScheme`.
  All three callable hooks are optional; at least one of them (or a
  custom `build_model`) should encode positional information, otherwise
  the Transformer will behave as NoPE.
- `build_model(config)` returns an `nn.Module` that exposes
  `forward(tokens) -> [B, T, V]` over `vocab_size(config)` tokens.
- Buffers / parameters created inside `build_positional_scheme` must be
  registered through `scheme.extra_modules` so they move with the model
  to GPU and are seen by the optimizer.

## Metric
For each variant the run reports `exact_match_id`, `token_acc_id`,
`exact_match_ood`, `token_acc_ood`, and a combined
`score = 0.5 * exact_match_id + 0.5 * exact_match_ood`.
The leaderboard aggregates these per variant; the task-level summary is
the geometric mean across the three variants, which penalises any single
variant where the model fails to length-generalise.

## Baselines
- **lstm_attn** — Bahdanau-style LSTM seq2seq (single-stream causal LM
  variant). The classic recurrent baseline.
- **transformer_sinusoidal** — Decoder-only Transformer with sinusoidal
  absolute PE (Vaswani et al., 2017).
- **transformer_alibi** — Decoder-only Transformer with ALiBi additive
  attention bias (Press, Smith & Lewis, ICLR 2022; arXiv:2108.12409).
- **transformer_nope** — Decoder-only Transformer with no positional
  encoding (Kazemnejad et al., NeurIPS 2023; arXiv:2305.19466). This is
  a strong length-OOD reference and probes the NoPE-vs-ALiBi tradeoff;
  in this release setup, `transformer_alibi` is expected to be strongest
  overall across the three exact-copy variants, while sinusoidal PE and
  the recurrent attention baseline are expected to be weak on OOD exact
  match.

tasks.name: Length-Generalizing Dyck Stack Model
tasks.summary: Studies how sequence architectures implement stack-like memory for bounded Dyck languages and length-out-of-distribution generalization.
tasks.description_md:
# Synthetic: Dyck-(k,m) Language Modelling

## Research Question
Can you design a sequence-model architecture that learns the **bounded
hierarchical Dyck-(k,m) language** — well-nested strings over `k` bracket
types with maximum nesting depth `m` — and, crucially, that
**length-generalizes** to test strings strictly longer than anything seen
during training?

## Background
Dyck-(k,m) is the canonical formal language for studying whether neural
sequence models can implement an *explicit stack*.  At every position of a
Dyck string the next valid tokens are determined entirely by the stack of
currently-open brackets, so an exact recognizer needs only `O(m log k)`
bits of memory (Hewitt, Hahn, Ganguli, Liang, Manning, EMNLP 2020,
[arXiv:2010.07515](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.07515)).  Yet vanilla LSTMs
and Transformers regularly fail to length-generalize on Dyck-(k,m): they
collapse from near-100% accuracy on in-distribution lengths down to
chance on longer test strings.  Adding an explicit differentiable stack
(Joulin & Mikolov, NeurIPS 2015, [arXiv:1503.01007](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01007);
Suzgun et al. 2019, [arXiv:1911.03329](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03329))
or a carefully designed positional encoding (Yao, Peng, Papadimitriou,
Narasimhan, ACL 2021, [arXiv:2105.11115](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11115))
restores generalization.  This task asks the agent to invent the
architectural fix.

## What You Can Modify
Edit only the `build_model(...)` function inside the editable block of
`pytorch-examples/synth_dyck/custom_strategy.py`.  Everything else —
the Dyck-(k,m) sampler, the vocabulary, the language-model training
loop (AdamW, cross-entropy on every position, gradient clipping), the
evaluation (next-valid-set token accuracy + per-string accuracy), and
the per-environment overrides — is fixed.

## Fixed Setup
- **Vocabulary** (size `2k + 2`): BOS, EOS/PAD, `k` open brackets, `k`
  matching close brackets.
- **Training corpus**: 8 000 strings sampled uniformly over even lengths
  in the per-environment training range, kept in memory.
- **Evaluation corpora**: 1 000 in-distribution strings (same length
  range as training) and 1 000 length-OOD strings (lengths strictly
  longer than the training maximum).
- **Loss**: token-level softmax cross-entropy over non-PAD positions.
- **Optimizer**: AdamW, `lr = 3e-3`, `weight_decay = 0`, gradient norm
  clipped to `1.0`.
- **Batch size**: 64.
- **Training budget**: 100 gradient steps per env.
- **Parameter budget**: `≤ 500 000` trainable parameters
  (`config.max_params`).  The harness raises an error if `build_model`
  exceeds this.
- **Runs per env**: 1 internal run per outer seed.

## Interface
`build_model(config: TaskConfig) -> DyckModel` must return a
`torch.nn.Module` subclass of `DyckModel` that exposes
`forward(input_ids: LongTensor[B, T]) -> logits: FloatTensor[B, T, vocab]`.
The model receives sequences of the form `[BOS, x1, …, xn, EOS, PAD, …]`
and is scored on its predictions at every non-PAD position.

## Fixed Setup
| label              | `k` | `m` | train length | OOD eval length |
|--------------------|-----|-----|--------------|-----------------|
| `dyck-k2-m3`       | 2   | 3   | [8, 64]      | [65, 96]        |
| `dyck-k8-m5`       | 8   | 5   | [16, 96]     | [97, 128]       |
| `dyck-length-ood`  | 4   | 4   | [8, 64]      | [128, 256]      |

The third environment is the hard length-OOD probe: training tops out
at length 64 and the model is tested on strings of length 128–256.

## Metrics
For each environment the parser writes the following columns to the
leaderboard:
- `id_token_acc_<env>` — token-level next-valid-set accuracy on the
  in-distribution split (higher is better, bounded in `[0, 1]`).
- `ood_token_acc_<env>` — same metric on the length-OOD split (this is
  the **headline** generalization score and the primary score column).
- `id_string_acc_<env>`, `ood_string_acc_<env>` — strict per-string
  accuracy (every position correct).
- `params_<env>` — number of trainable parameters reported by
  `MODEL_INFO`.

Per-env scores use `ood_token_acc`; the task score is the geometric mean
across the three environments.

## Baselines and Expected Ordering
1. **`lstm`** — 2-layer LSTM language model (Hewitt et al. EMNLP 2020,
   [arXiv:2010.07515](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.07515)).  Strong on
   in-distribution `dyck-k2-m3` but degrades sharply on length-OOD
   (vanilla LSTM mean 1.39% on Dyck-2 OOD per Suzgun et al. 2019, Table 2,
   [arXiv:1911.03329](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03329)).
2. **`transformer`** — 4-layer causal Transformer with learned absolute
   positional embeddings (Yao et al. ACL 2021,
   [arXiv:2105.11115](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.11115)).  Section 6.2
   of that paper reports >99.9% validation accuracy on Dyck-(k,D)
   across `k ∈ {2, 8, 32, 128}, D ∈ {3, 5, 10, 15}` but length
   generalization depends critically on the positional encoding;
   learned/sinusoidal absolute embeddings typically fail OOD.
3. **`stack_rnn`** — SOTA: Stack-augmented RNN with softmax PUSH/POP/NO-OP
   actions, following Joulin & Mikolov, NeurIPS 2015
   ([arXiv:1503.01007](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01007)) and the
   `Stack-RNN+Softmax` variant of Suzgun et al. 2019
   ([arXiv:1911.03329](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.03329), Tables 2 and 4:
   mean 99.99% on Dyck-2 OOD and 99.85% on Dyck-6 OOD).

**Expected partial ordering** (length-OOD token accuracy):

    stack_rnn  >  transformer  ≈  lstm   (on length-OOD splits)
    transformer ≈ stack_rnn ≈ lstm        (on in-distribution splits)

## Hints
- The hard part is OOD generalization; matching LSTM in-distribution
  accuracy is not enough.
- An explicit, length-independent state (a soft stack, a relative
  positional encoding, NoPE with future-masking, ALiBi, …) is the
  documented way to close the OOD gap.
- The parameter budget (`config.max_params = 500 000`) is generous for
  small RNNs/Transformers but rules out very wide models — favour
  inductive bias over scale.

tasks.summary: Studies how initialization, optimization, and refits let two-layer MLPs recover single-index directions and links.
tasks.description_md:
# Synthetic Single-Index Recovery

## Research Question
Design a training recipe (initialisation + per-step optimisation + optional
post-hoc refit) for a fixed two-layer ReLU MLP that recovers the *index
direction* `theta*` and the *link* `g` of a single-index model
`y = g(<theta*, x>) + noise` across multiple link families.

## Background
A single-index model assumes the target depends on the input only through a
one-dimensional projection. It is a classical semi-parametric workhorse and
the simplest non-trivial model where neural networks must perform *feature
learning* (going beyond the kernel regime). Three results frame the
problem:

* **Ben Arous, Gheissari, Jagannath**, *Online stochastic gradient descent
  on non-convex losses from high-dimensional inference*, JMLR 22 (2021),
  arXiv:2003.10409 -- introduces the *information exponent* `k` of `g`
  and shows online SGD on a single neuron needs `n = Omega(d^{k-1})`
  samples for weak recovery.
* **Bietti, Bruna, Sanford, Song**, *Learning Single-Index Models with
  Shallow Neural Networks*, NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2210.15651 -- shows that
  a *frozen-bias* two-layer ReLU net (biases sampled at init, never
  trained) has a benign landscape and attains near-optimal
  semi-parametric sample complexity for any link with `k >= 1`.
* **Damian, Lee, Soltanolkotabi**, *Neural Networks can Learn
  Representations with Gradient Descent*, COLT 2022, arXiv:2206.15144 --
  shows that **one giant gradient step** on the first layer (followed
  by a ridge readout) learns the relevant direction with
  `n = O(d^2)` samples, beating the kernel rate `n = O(d^p)`.

The benchmark covers three link functions of increasing difficulty:

| Label          | `g(z)`           | Information exponent `k` |
|----------------|------------------|--------------------------|
| `relu-d100`    | `ReLU(z)`        | 1 (easy)                 |
| `hermite-d100` | `He_3(z)/sqrt(6)`| 3 (hard, beyond kernel)  |
| `sign-d100`    | `sign(z)`        | non-smooth, robustness   |

All three environments use `d = 100` (well inside the safe wall-clock
budget on one H100) and Gaussian inputs `x ~ N(0, I_d)`.

## What You Can Modify
Edit `pytorch-examples/synth_single_index/custom_strategy.py` only inside
the `EDITABLE` block. Everything else (data generator, model class,
evaluation, driver, link functions) is fixed.

The editable block must export `build_strategy(config)`, returning an
object with four callbacks:

| Callback                                       | Contract                                                                                                  |
|------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `init_two_layer(net, config)`                  | Initialise `net.fc1`, `net.fc2` (any in-place scheme allowed); may freeze parameters via `requires_grad_` |
| `make_optimizer(net, config) -> Optimizer`     | Return a `torch.optim.Optimizer` controlling the trainable parameters                                     |
| `training_step(net, opt, x, y, step, cfg)`     | Run one update on the given mini-batch and return `StepMetrics(loss=..., extra=...)`                      |
| `finalize(net, x_train, y_train, config)`      | Optional global refit (e.g. closed-form ridge readout) after the step budget is exhausted                 |

You may NOT change `TwoLayerMLP`, the data generator, the link
functions, the evaluation function, or the driver.

## Fixed Setup
* Model: `TwoLayerMLP = Linear(d, W) -> ReLU -> Linear(W, 1)` with
  `W = 256`.
* Inputs: `x ~ N(0, I_d)` with `d = 100`.
* Noise: zero-mean Gaussian with `sigma = 0.1` (training only;
  test target is noise-free).
* Per environment: one internal replica per top-level seed (different
  `theta*` and data draws), trained from scratch. The release config uses
  three top-level seeds.
* Wall-clock budget: well under 30 minutes per (baseline x env) on a
  single H100 with `d = 100`.

## Metrics
For each environment we report:

* `test_mse_<env>`     -- mean squared error on a 8192-point noise-free
                           test set (lower is better).
* `direction_recovery_<env>` = `|<theta_hat, theta*>|` for that replica
                           (higher is better; 1 == perfect).
* `score_<env>` = `direction_recovery_<env>` (the primary signal).

`theta_hat` is computed from the trained network as
`theta_hat = normalize(sum_j |a_j| * w_j)` where `w_j` are the first-layer
rows and `a_j` the readout weights -- the standard direction estimator
used by Bietti et al. (2022).

## Baselines
* **sgd_mlp** -- vanilla 2-layer ReLU MLP + SGD with momentum, Kaiming
  init (Bietti et al. 2022 reference baseline).
* **frozen_bias** -- shallow network with biases frozen at random init
  (Bietti et al. 2022, Theorem 1; achieves near-optimal sample
  complexity for any information exponent).
* **damian_giant_step** -- *one giant gradient step* on the first layer
  + spherical projection + closed-form ridge readout on the resulting
  features (Damian, Lee, Soltanolkotabi 2022). This is the SOTA
  baseline; it is the only baseline that provably beats the kernel rate
  on the Hermite link.

## Expected Ordering (from theory)
For the Hermite link (information exponent `k = 3`):

```
damian_giant_step  >  frozen_bias  >  sgd_mlp
```

For the ReLU link (`k = 1`) all three should recover the direction; the
SGD baseline often catches up.

For the sign link none of the three is provably consistent; we report it
mainly as a robustness probe.

## Hints
* The Hermite link's loss landscape has a long plateau before the
  direction "snaps in". Either use a very small step size for many
  iterations, or take a single large step on the first-layer weights
  followed by a closed-form readout.
* Restricting the first-layer rows to the unit sphere (project after
  each update) keeps the gradient signal-to-noise ratio bounded.
* Bias engineering matters: random-then-frozen biases (Bietti 2022)
  are a strong, well-conditioned default.

tasks.summary: Studies how sequence models simulate finite-state semiautomata across shortcut-solvable and harder random-DFA regimes.
tasks.description_md:
# Synth-Semiautomata: architectures for finite-state simulation

## Research Question
What sequence-model architecture lets a *non-recurrent* (or weakly-recurrent)
network simulate a finite-state semiautomaton `A = (Q, Σ, δ)` end-to-end,
across the regimes where shortcut solutions exist *and* where they
provably should not?

A semiautomaton produces a state sequence `q_t = δ(q_{t-1}, σ_t)`. Liu et al.
2022 ("Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata", arXiv:2210.10749, ICLR 2023)
prove that **(a)** every semiautomaton admits an `O(log T)`-depth Transformer
simulator (Thm 1); **(b)** *solvable* semiautomata admit constant-depth
simulators via Krohn–Rhodes decomposition (Thm 2); but **(c)** non-solvable
semiautomata (the smallest example generates `A_5`, the alternating group on
5 letters) provably do **not** admit constant-depth shortcuts unless
`TC^0 = NC^1` (Thm 4). Empirically, Figure 8 in their paper shows depth-1
GPT-2 already reaches 99.8% on the 1D grid world and the parity counter,
while non-solvable `S_5` is stuck at 7.9% (depth 1) and needs ~depth 12-16
to clear 99% (max over 20 runs).

## Background
We expose three synthetic environments that cover both regimes:

1. **`memory_unit`** — `K`-state memory unit: alphabet `{noop, write(0), …,
   write(K-1)}`. `noop` keeps the state; `write(j)` jumps to state `j`. The
   transformation semigroup is the constant-function semigroup; Krohn–Rhodes
   theory shows it is one of the two "primes" used to factorize *any*
   solvable semiautomaton (Liu et al. 2022, §3.1). Depth-1 Transformer is
   theoretically sufficient.
2. **`grid_world`** — `Grid_n`: states `{0, …, n-1}` on a line, alphabet
   `{L, R}`, reflecting (clamping) boundaries. Liu et al. 2022 Thm 3 gives
   an `O(1)`-depth, `O(1)`-embedding self-attention construction. Their
   experiments report ≥99.8% test accuracy at depth-1 on `Grid_9`
   (Figure 8 / Figure 3a) and 100% from depth-2 onward.
3. **`random_dfa`** — a random transition table `δ : Q × Σ → Q` with
   `|Q|=60`, `|Σ|=8`, length `T=40`. Random transitions on 60 states
   typically generate a transformation semigroup containing `S_5` (which is
   non-solvable), placing this environment in the regime where no
   constant-depth shortcut exists — the analog of the hardest row of
   Liu et al. 2022 Figure 8.

## What You Can Modify
Edit only the editable block of
`pytorch-examples/synth_semiautomata/custom_strategy.py`, which exposes:

```python
def build_model(env_spec: EnvSpec, config: TaskConfig) -> nn.Module: ...
def get_optimizer_config(config: TaskConfig) -> dict[str, float]: ...
def forward_logits(model, input_ids, env_spec) -> torch.Tensor: ...
```

`build_model` must return an `nn.Module` mapping
`input_ids ∈ {0, …, env_spec.alphabet_size-1}^{B×T}` to per-position state
logits of shape `[B, T, env_spec.num_states]`. `forward_logits` is the
inference wrapper (use it to implement looped / scratchpad-style
architectures that don't fit the plain `model(x)` signature). The optimizer
must be AdamW with the four hyperparameters returned by
`get_optimizer_config`.

## Fixed Setup
- Per-token cross-entropy loss against full state sequences `q_{1:T}`.
- Online training with freshly sampled batches each step (matches
  Liu et al. 2022 App. B.1.1 — "online learning setting … this is to
  mitigate the orthogonal challenge of overfitting").
- `memory_unit`: K=8 states, sequence length 40, 8000 training steps.
- `grid_world`: n=9 states (`Grid_9`), sequence length 40, 8000 steps.
- `random_dfa`: |Q|=60, |Σ|=8, sequence length 40, 12000 steps.
- Batch size 64, gradient clipping at 1.0, early stop after 3 consecutive
  log windows at training accuracy ≥0.999.
- Evaluation: 32 freshly sampled batches with held-out seed; reports mean
  per-token state-prediction accuracy.

## Metric
The leaderboard metric per environment is `test_accuracy` (also emitted as
`score`). Higher is better; bounded in `[0, 1]`. The aggregate task score is
the geometric mean across the three environments, so all three must be
strong.

## Baselines (variants of the architecture)
- **transformer** — depth-1 GPT-2-style causal Transformer, `d_model=128`,
  4 heads (Liu et al. 2022 App. B.3 use `d=512, 8 heads` for their main
  experiments; we use a smaller width to fit the per-env wall-time budget).
- **lstm** — single-layer LSTM with embedding 64 and hidden dim 128
  (matches Liu et al. 2022 App. B.3 LSTM recipe; reported as the
  "depth-T recurrent reference" that reaches 100% on all settings,
  Figure 5a / Figure 11).
- **looped_transformer** *(SOTA candidate)* — single shared Transformer
  block applied for 6 loops (Giannou et al. 2023, "Looped Transformers as
  Programmable Computers", arXiv:2301.13196). Provides effective depth 6
  at the parameter count of a 1-layer model, the regime in which
  Liu et al. 2022 Figure 8 column-6 starts to be competitive on non-solvable
  groups (`A_5`: 99.3%; `S_5`: 28.4%).

## Hints
- For `random_dfa`, depth (or loop count) is the dominant lever; Liu et al.
  2022 Thm 4 shows constant-depth Transformers provably cannot simulate
  non-solvable transformation semigroups, so any architecture that does not
  scale its sequential compute with `|Q|` or `T` will plateau well below the
  LSTM ceiling.
- For `grid_world`, the Liu et al. 2022 Thm 3 construction is depth-2 with
  attention dimension `O(1)` and MLP width `O(T)`. Even a tiny model
  should saturate ≥99%.
- Positional encoding matters for length generalization (Liu et al. 2022
  Figure 15) but we evaluate only at the training length, so the default
  learned embeddings are fine.

tasks.name: Sparse Staircase Function Learning
tasks.summary: Studies how two-layer networks and training rules learn sparse hypercube functions across MSP and leap-complexity regimes.
tasks.description_md:
# Synth-Staircase: Learning Sparse Functions on the Hypercube

## Research Question
For a two-layer fully connected neural network of width `M` trained by online
batch-SGD on the hypercube `{+1, -1}^d`, can you design the model
(architecture / initialization / parametrization), the optimizer, and the
training step so that the network learns the latent target

```
f*(x) = h*(x_{j_1}, ..., x_{j_P})
```

across the full range of "hierarchy levels" of the latent target `h*`, in
particular for the leap-1 (MSP) staircase, the leap-2 non-MSP chain, and the
leap-3 monomial?

## Background
Abbe, Boix-Adsera, and Misiakiewicz (COLT 2022, arXiv:2202.08658) introduced
the **merged-staircase property (MSP)**: a sparse latent target
`h* : {+1, -1}^P -> R` with non-zero Fourier coefficients indexed by
`S = {S_1, ..., S_m}` satisfies MSP iff the supports can be ordered so that
`|S_i \ ∪_{j<i} S_j| <= 1` for every `i`. They prove that MSP is both
**necessary and nearly sufficient** for a two-layer mean-field SGD network
to learn `f*` in `O(d)` samples in the ambient-dimension `d` regime; for
non-MSP targets the dimension-free dynamics are stuck at strictly positive
risk (Theorem 7 of the paper). A follow-up (Abbe, Boix-Adsera, Misiakiewicz,
COLT 2023, arXiv:2302.11055) extended this with the **leap complexity**: a
leap-`k` function is conjectured (and partially proven) to be learnable in
`Theta(d^max(k,2))` SGD steps via saddle-to-saddle dynamics.

Linear / kernel methods on any fixed feature map (NTK, random features)
provably cannot learn `k`-sparse parities with fewer than `Omega(d^k)`
samples (Ghorbani-Mei-Misiakiewicz-Montanari, Ann. Stat. 2021;
Hsu-Sanford-Servedio-Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis 2021), so even the easiest
component `z1 z2 z3` of `h1` and the leap-3 target `h3` are out of reach
for the NTK baseline at our sample budget.

## What You Can Modify
Edit the scaffold file `pytorch-examples/synth_staircase/custom_strategy.py`
only inside the editable block containing the three functions:

1. `build_model(config)` — returns the trainable `nn.Module`. The module
   must take an input of shape `[batch_size, d]` (with entries in
   `{+1, -1}`) and return a tensor of shape `[batch_size]` or
   `[batch_size, 1]`.
2. `get_optimizer(model, config)` — returns the `torch.optim.Optimizer`
   used to update the model.
3. `train_step(model, optimizer, x, y)` — one gradient update on a fresh
   batch `(x, y)`; must return a Python `float` training loss.

The data sampler (uniform on `{+1, -1}^d`), the targets `h1`, `h2`, `h3`,
the loss (squared error vs the target value), and the evaluation pipeline
are all FIXED inside the harness and must not be modified.

## Fixed Setup
- Ambient dimension `d = 100`, latent dimension `P = 4`.
- Batch size `b = 150`, total online-SGD steps `T = 4 000` per run
  (one-pass: every batch is freshly sampled from the uniform distribution
  on `{+1, -1}^d`).
- Width `M = 100`.
- Three latent targets, one per evaluation environment:
  - `h1(z) = z1 + z1 z2 + z1 z2 z3` — vanilla staircase, MSP / leap-1.
  - `h2(z) = z1 z2 + z2 z3 + z3 z4` — non-MSP chain with leap-2.
  - `h3(z) = z1 z2 z3` — pure monomial, leap-3, non-staircase.
- One independent run per environment per top-level seed with a different
  latent subset `I`, reported as test MSE and Fourier-coefficient recovery.
  The release config uses three top-level seeds.

## Interface Notes
- `build_model` must construct a fresh model — the harness re-creates one
  for each run.
- `get_optimizer` must wrap only `model.parameters()` (or a filtered
  subset).
- `train_step` must perform a single optimizer step and return the
  scalar training loss as a Python `float`.
- The harness clears gradients automatically only via your code: you must
  call `optimizer.zero_grad()` inside `train_step`.
- Everything is run inside one Python process per environment per seed.

## Metric
For each environment we report:

- `test_mse_{env}` — MSE of `model(x)` against `h*(x_I)` on `8192` fresh
  test samples (lower is better).
- `fourier_recovery_{env}` — mean `|hat_S(model) - hat_S(h*)|` over the
  latent monomials `S` (lower is better).
- `score_{env} = exp(-test_mse_{env})` — bounded in `(0, 1]`, higher is
  better; this is the primary leaderboard metric.

The aggregate task score is the geometric mean of the three per-environment
scores. A catastrophic failure on `h3` is not papered over by a great
result on `h1`.

## Baselines (variants of the reference setup)
- **mean_field_sgd** — Two-layer fully-connected network with shifted
  sigmoid activation `sigma(x) = (1 + exp(-x + 0.5))^(-1)`, no trainable
  first-layer bias, `a_j ~ Unif({+1, -1})`, `w_j ~ N(0, I_d)` at
  initialization, plain SGD with `lr = 0.5`. This
  exactly matches the experimental setup of Abbe-Boix-Adsera-Misiakiewicz
  COLT 2022 Figure 1 (`d = N = 100`, `b = 150`, `eta = 1/2`). Provably
  strong on `h1` (MSP), provably stuck on `h2` / `h3` in the `O(d)`-sample
  mean-field regime.
- **ntk** — Same architecture but with NTK-style first layer
  (`w ~ N(0, 1/d)`, `b ~ N(0, 1)`) FROZEN at initialization; only the
  readout is trained (the canonical lazy / random-features baseline of
  Jacot-Gabriel-Hongler NeurIPS 2018). By the linear-method lower bound
  of Ghorbani-Mei-Misiakiewicz-Montanari (Ann. Stat. 2021), this needs
  `Omega(d^k)` samples to learn leap-`k` structure and is expected to fail on
  `h2` and `h3` at our budget.
- **curriculum_layerwise** — SOTA candidate that combines mu-P-style
  initialization (Yang-Hu 2020), shifted-sigmoid activation with nonzero low
  derivatives near the origin, Adam with per-layer learning rates, and
  layer-wise alternating updates to drive saddle-to-saddle dynamics
  (Abbe-Boix-Adsera-Misiakiewicz, COLT 2023, arXiv:2302.11055). Expected
  to dominate `mean_field_sgd` on `h2` (leap-2).

## Hints
- The model uses input `x in {+1, -1}^d`, NOT `{0, 1}^d`; this matches
  the Fourier-Walsh convention used by Abbe et al. and is what makes the
  monomial-decomposition / Fourier-recovery metric meaningful.
- The leap-`k` conjecture predicts that ANY hierarchical strategy that
  follows the leap ordering can learn `h2` in `O(d^2)` and `h3` in
  `O(d^3)` SGD steps. With `T = 4000` and `d = 100` this is enough to
  resolve `h2` but at the boundary for `h3` — perfect recovery on `h3` is
  HARD and is the discriminator between baselines.
- Tools that help with non-MSP targets: width scaling, smoother
  activations with non-zero higher derivatives at `0`, layer-wise
  optimization, adaptive optimizers (Adam / muP), or explicit
  curriculum / leap-ordering of the loss.

tasks.name: Multi-Index Feature Learning Strategy
tasks.summary: Studies how training recipes for two-layer MLPs recover hidden low-dimensional teacher subspaces in multi-index models.
tasks.description_md:
# Synth Multi-Index

## Research Question
Can you design a training recipe for a *fixed* two-layer ReLU MLP that
recovers the hidden r-dimensional teacher subspace `U* ∈ R^{d×r}` and
learns the unknown link function `g`, when the target is

```
y = g(U*ᵀ x),   x ~ N(0, I_d).
```

You may only modify (i) parameter initialization, (ii) training-data
construction, (iii) optimizer hyperparameters, and (iv) the per-step
update rule. The network architecture (Linear → ReLU → Linear), width,
batch size, training budget, and evaluation protocol are fixed.

## Background
Multi-index models, where labels depend on the input only through a
low-dimensional projection `U*ᵀ x`, are a canonical setting for studying
how neural networks discover low-dimensional structure. Three lines of
recent work give concrete recipes that recover `U*` faster than vanilla
SGD on a randomly initialized MLP:

* **Mean-field Langevin dynamics** — Mousavi-Hosseini, Wu, Erdogdu
  (ICLR 2025; [arXiv:2408.07254](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07254))
  show that two-layer networks trained with noisy gradient descent and
  KL-style weight decay achieve sample complexity that grows *almost
  linearly with the effective subspace dimension* `d_eff`, bypassing
  the information-exponent bottleneck of single-loss SGD.
* **Layer-wise / two-stage training** — Bietti, Bruna, Sanford
  (NeurIPS 2022) and Dandi *et al.*, "How Two-Layer Neural Networks
  Learn, One (Giant) Step at a Time"
  ([JMLR 2024](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume25/23-1543/23-1543.pdf))
  fit the first layer with spherical SGD on a correlation loss, then
  solve for the output weights in closed form by ridge regression.
* **Leap-complexity SGD** — Abbe, Boix-Adserà, Misiakiewicz
  ([COLT 2023; arXiv:2302.11055](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.11055))
  characterize how staircase / hierarchical link functions are learned
  by SGD in a *saddle-to-saddle* dynamic, motivating leap-aware schedules
  for staged learning.

The benchmark uses link `g(z) = (1/√r) · Σ_i He₃(z_i)` (a sum of cubic
Hermite polynomials) with information exponent 3. With `d = 128`, vanilla
SGD on a fresh dataset of `n = 4096` points stalls; the SOTA recipes
should reach much lower test MSE and a near-zero subspace error.

## What You Can Modify
Edit `pytorch-examples/synth_multi_index/custom_strategy.py` only inside
the editable block containing:

1. `init_model(model, config)`
2. `make_dataset(config, teacher, seed)`
3. `get_optimizer_config(config)`
4. `training_step(model, optimizer, optimizer_config, batch_x, batch_y, step, config)`

The fixed driver constructs the MLP, calls `init_model`, builds the
optimizer from `get_optimizer_config`, samples `make_dataset` once per
teacher, then iterates `training_step` for `max_steps = 8000` mini-batch
updates.

## Fixed Setup
* Inputs: `x ∈ R^d` with `x ~ N(0, I_d)`.
* Targets: `y = (1/√r) · Σ_{i=1..r} He₃((U*ᵀ x)_i)`, where `He₃(z) = z³ − 3z`.
* Teacher: column-orthonormal `U* ∈ R^{d×r}` sampled from the Haar measure.
* Model: `Linear(d, 256) → ReLU → Linear(256, 1)` (bias on both layers).
* Loss: per-batch mean squared error.
* Batch size: 128.
* Training budget: 8 000 mini-batch steps.
* Evaluation: one teacher and one data ordering per top-level seed in the
  release configuration. The config uses three top-level seeds for the
  leaderboard mean.
* Allowed maximum training-set size: `max_train_examples = 200_000`.

## Fixed Setup
The same scaffold is evaluated at three teacher ranks:

| Label | `d` | `r` | Notes |
|-------|-----|-----|-------|
| `r2`  | 128 | 2   | Easiest — small subspace, easiest to recover |
| `r3`  | 128 | 3   | Moderate |
| `r4`  | 128 | 4   | Hardest — larger subspace; more directions to align |

## Interface Notes
* `init_model(...)` must not look at the teacher subspace; it only sees
  the model and the `TaskConfig`. The teacher is passed to `make_dataset`
  solely as the label oracle.
* `make_dataset(...)` may return either `(x, y)` or `{"x": x, "y": y}`.
  `x` must have shape `[n, d]` with finite floats and `y` must have
  shape `[n]` (or `[n, 1]`).
* `get_optimizer_config(...)` must return a dict containing `optimizer`
  (`"sgd"` or `"adamw"`), `lr_inner`, `lr_outer`, `wd_inner`, `wd_outer`,
  `momentum`, and `noise_std`. Inner/outer refer to the first
  (`d → W`) and second (`W → 1`) linear layers.
* `training_step(...)` is called once per mini-batch. It should perform
  exactly one optimizer update and return a dict with at least `loss`.
  You may freeze parts of the model, project rows onto the unit sphere,
  inject Langevin noise (multiply `optimizer_config.noise_std` by
  `sqrt(2*lr)` for the SDE discretization), or run a stage-2 closed-form
  ridge solve.

## Metrics
The driver prints one `TEST_METRICS` line per run with three values:

| Metric | Direction | Definition |
|--------|-----------|------------|
| `test_mse` | lower better | MSE on a fresh 8 192-point test set |
| `subspace_err` | lower better | `||P_Uhat − P_U*||_F`, where `Uhat` is the top-`r` right singular subspace of the first layer's weights |
| `score` | higher better | `exp(-subspace_err² / r) · exp(-test_mse)`, in (0, 1] |

The leaderboard aggregates `score`, `test_mse`, and `subspace_err`
across the three rank settings via the standard geometric mean of
per-rank weighted-mean composites (see `score_spec.py`).

## Baselines (variants of the reference setup)
* **sgd_mlp** — vanilla joint SGD on both layers, Kaiming init, no
  noise, no weight decay; the reference two-layer SGD baseline studied by
  Abbe, Boix-Adserà, Misiakiewicz ([arXiv:2302.11055](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.11055)).
* **two_stage** — first layer trained by spherical SGD on a correlation
  loss while the output layer is held fixed, then the output layer is
  refitted by ridge regression on the post-ReLU features
  (Bietti *et al.* NeurIPS 2022; Dandi *et al.* JMLR 2024).
* **mean_field_langevin (SOTA)** — noisy SGD with KL-style weight decay
  in the mean-field parametrization, implementing the discretized
  Langevin diffusion of Mousavi-Hosseini, Wu, Erdogdu
  ([arXiv:2408.07254](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07254)).

## Hints
* Hermite-3 has information exponent 3, so a single-loss SGD step gets
  a `O(1/√d)` signal in each teacher direction. Methods that exploit
  the population gradient over a fresh-sample pool, project to the
  sphere, or stage feature learning before fitting the output layer
  recover the subspace dramatically faster.
* `subspace_err` is upper-bounded by `√(2r)`; values near `√(2r)` mean
  no recovery, values close to zero mean perfect recovery.
* Increasing `r` makes the partial-ordering of methods more pronounced:
  on `r4`, vanilla SGD typically fails (`subspace_err` close to the
  random baseline), while staged or Langevin recipes degrade gracefully.

tasks.name: Flip-Flop State-Tracking Architecture
tasks.summary: Studies how sequence architectures avoid rare read errors in flip-flop language modeling, especially on long sparse tails.
tasks.description_md:
# Synth Flip-Flop Language Modeling

## Research Question
Design a causal sequence-model architecture (or attention modification) that, with all training data, optimizer, and evaluation pipeline held fixed, **eliminates the rare-but-persistent read errors** that vanilla Transformers exhibit when modelling the flip-flop language of Liu et al. 2023 — especially on the **long sparse tail** of the input distribution.

## Background
The flip-flop language `FFL(T, p)` of Liu, Ash, Goel, Krishnamurthy, Zhang ("Exposing Attention Glitches with Flip-Flop Language Modeling", NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2306.00946) is the simplest non-trivial state-tracking language. Each token is a (instruction, bit) pair from
```
Sigma = { w0, w1, i0, i1, r0, r1 }
```
where
- `w b` writes bit `b` to a 1-bit memory;
- `i b` is an *ignore* with a random visible bit; the memory does not change;
- `r b` is a *read*: the second symbol `b` is constrained to be the current memory state, and the model is graded on whether it predicts the read bit correctly.

The triple `(p_w, p_r, p_i)` controls the distribution. The paper's canonical training distribution is `FFL(T=512, p_i=0.8)` (so `p_w = p_r = 0.1`). Out-of-distribution evaluation amplifies the rare tail behaviours:
- `FFL(p_i=0.98)` — sparse: long stretches of ignore, the read sees a write at a distance often > 100 tokens (the failure mode for vanilla Transformers).
- `FFL(p_i=0.5)` — dense: writes are common; the most-recent write is usually within a few tokens.
- A long-context variant (T = 1024) at the training distribution.

Liu et al. report that vanilla Transformers exhibit *attention glitches*: rare but persistent read errors whose probability does not vanish with scaling or with training data, while a 1-layer LSTM achieves **exactly 0 OOD error on 100/100 replicates** (Section B.2, result R2). Mamba-style state-space models inherit the same recurrent inductive bias (Gu & Dao 2023, arXiv:2312.00752) and trivially solve FFLM-class state-tracking; see also Mamba-3 (arXiv:2603.15569, Section on Parity).

## Task
Edit `pytorch-examples/synth_flip_flop/custom_strategy.py` **only inside the editable block** (the `class FlipFlopModel(nn.Module)` plus the `build_model(config)` factory, lines 191-241 of the scaffold). Everything else — data generation, training loop, optimizer, evaluation — is FIXED and must not be modified.

The fixed training loop runs for 3000 steps on freshly sampled `FFL(p_i=0.8, T=512)` batches with AdamW (lr=3e-4, wd=0.1, batch_size=16), then evaluates on three OOD splits.

## Interface
- Implement a `torch.nn.Module` whose `forward(tokens)` accepts a `LongTensor` of shape `[batch, seq_len]` (token ids in 0..5) and returns a `FloatTensor` of shape `[batch, seq_len, 6]` of next-token logits.
- The model **must be causal**: position `t` depends only on positions `<= t`.
- The model must handle sequence lengths up to 1024 (used for the long-context eval).
- Total trainable parameters should stay below 50M.
- Provide a `build_model(config: TaskConfig) -> nn.Module` factory that the fixed driver calls.
- The model is graded on **read positions only**: a prediction is wrong iff `argmax(logits[t])` does not equal the read-bit target `tokens[t+1]` when `tokens[t+1] in {r0=4, r1=5}`. The headline metric is `seq_error_rate` = fraction of evaluation sequences with at least one read error; the `score` reported per environment is `1 - seq_error_rate`.

## Fixed Setup
- Vocab: `{w0=0, w1=1, i0=2, i1=3, r0=4, r1=5}` (6 tokens total).
- Training distribution: `FFL(T=512, p_i=0.8)`, online sampling.
- Optimizer: AdamW with `lr=3e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.999), wd=0.1, warmup=50, linear decay`.
- Batch size: 16, max steps: 3000, gradient clipping at 1.0.
- Loss: cross-entropy over the full next-token distribution at every position.
- Three OOD eval splits, each scored independently:
  - `dense` (`FFL(p_i=0.5, T=512)`, 2000 sequences)
  - `sparse` (`FFL(p_i=0.98, T=512)`, 2000 sequences) — the headline tail
  - `long_ctx` (`FFL(p_i=0.8, T=1024)`, 500 sequences)

## Metric
Per environment:
- `score = 1 - seq_error_rate` (higher is better, bounded in [0, 1])
- `read_error_rate` = errors / total reads (lower is better)
- `seq_error_rate` = sequences with >= 1 read error / total sequences (lower is better)

The overall task score is the geometric mean of the per-environment scores. The most interesting split is `sparse`, where Liu et al. (2023) document the vanilla-Transformer failure mode.

## Baselines (literature references)
- **transformer** — 4-layer, 8-head, d_model=256 vanilla causal Transformer. Mirrors the "canonical baseline" of Liu et al. (NeurIPS 2023, Section 4). Expected to make rare but persistent errors on the sparse tail.
- **lstm** — 1-layer LSTM, hidden=128. Liu et al. report 0 OOD error on 100/100 replicates with this architecture (NeurIPS 2023, Section B.2 (R2), https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/510ad3018bbdc5b6e3b10646e2e35771-Paper-Conference.pdf ).
- **attn_sharp** — 4-layer Transformer with attention-sharpening (low-temperature softmax). Mirrors the strongest indirect mitigation reported in Liu et al. Section 4.2 / Figure 3 ("ent. attn sharp", "L attn sharp", "L2 attn sharp"). Improves on `sparse` over vanilla Transformer but does not fully close the gap.
- **ssm** — Pure-PyTorch Mamba-style selective diagonal SSM (Gu & Dao 2023, arXiv:2312.00752). The selective recurrent state trivially represents a 1-bit memory, so the SSM is expected to behave like the LSTM skyline (near-zero error on all splits).

## Hints
- The single-bit memory is *trivially* representable as a recurrent state. The question is which inductive biases let an autoregressive model converge to that representation under the fixed training distribution.
- Attention-sharpening, hard / sparse attention, peaked softmax temperatures, and explicit positional biases are documented as partial mitigations in the paper.
- Architectural changes (replace attention with a recurrence) are documented as full mitigations.
- You may not change the training data, the number of steps, the optimizer, or the evaluation loop.

tasks.name: Sub-Quadratic Associative Recall Mixer
tasks.summary: Studies how sequence-mixing modules perform in-context key-value lookup for long-context multi-query associative recall.
tasks.description_md:
# Synthetic Associative Recall (MQAR)

## Research Question
Design a **single sub-quadratic sequence-mixing module** (`CustomMixer`) that
solves Multi-Query Associative Recall (MQAR) at long context lengths. The
benchmark fixes everything else (embedding, residual stack, optimizer, data
generation, evaluation), so any accuracy gain must come from the mixer's
ability to perform in-context key-value lookups.

## Background
Associative recall has been the canonical synthetic stress-test for sequence
models since Graves et al.'s Neural Turing Machine (arXiv:1410.5401, 2014).
The modern variant we use here is **Multi-Query Associative Recall (MQAR)**
introduced by Arora, Eyuboglu et al. "Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall
in Efficient Language Models" (arXiv:2312.04927, 2023, Section 4.3): a stream
of `(key, value)` token pairs is followed by query keys, and the model must
emit the matching value at each query position.

Zoology's headline finding (Figure 2) is that **full softmax attention solves
MQAR at 100% accuracy with a constant model dimension (d=64)**, whereas
gated-convolution mixers (H3, Hyena, RWKV-v4, BaseConv) need their hidden
dimension to scale at least linearly with sequence length. Subsequent work
(BASED — Arora et al. 2024, arXiv:2402.18668; Mamba — Gu & Dao 2023,
arXiv:2312.00752) frames MQAR as **the** recall benchmark for the
recall-throughput Pareto frontier among sub-quadratic mixers: state-space
models like Mamba lose accuracy on MQAR as the KV-pair count grows because
they must compress all keys into a fixed-size hidden state, while spiky
input-dependent linear attention (BASED) closes most of the gap.

## What You Can Modify
Edit **only** the `CustomMixer` class in
`pytorch-examples/synth_associative_recall/custom_strategy.py`. The fixed
scaffold wires it as the **second** layer of a 2-layer Transformer-style
stack whose first layer is a short causal convolution (matching Zoology's
canonical hybrid setup).

`CustomMixer` must:
- Subclass `nn.Module`.
- Have constructor signature `__init__(self, d_model: int, seq_len: int, ...)`
  (extra keyword arguments are allowed with defaults).
- `forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor` taking and returning a
  tensor of shape `[batch, seq_len, d_model]`.
- Be **causal**: output at position `t` may only depend on inputs at
  positions `<= t`.

You may use anything from `torch`, `torch.nn`, `torch.nn.functional`, and
`math`.

## Fixed Setup
- **Task generator**: `multiquery_ar(...)` ported verbatim from Hazy
  Research's Zoology repo (MIT license,
  `zoology/data/multiquery_ar.py`).
- **Model wrapper**: `embed -> Block(ShortConv) -> Block(CustomMixer) -> head`,
  where each `Block` is `pre-norm residual mixer + pre-norm residual MLP`.
- **Hidden dim**: `d_model=64`, MLP expansion 2x, **tied** input/output embeddings.
- **Vocab**: `vocab_size = 8192` (matches Zoology Section 4.3 setup).
- **Optimizer**: `AdamW(lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.1, betas=(0.9, 0.95))` with
  cosine decay to `0.1 * lr`.
- **Loss**: token-level cross-entropy with `ignore_index=-100` (so only the
  query positions contribute).

## Fixed Setup

| Label | seq_len | num_kv_pairs | num_train_examples | epochs | batch |
|-------|--------:|-------------:|-------------------:|-------:|------:|
| `mqar-128`  | 128  | 8   | 20000 | 32 | 64 |
| `mqar-512`  | 512  | 32  | 20000 | 32 | 32 |
| `mqar-2048` | 2048 | 128 | 8000  | 16 | 16 |

The `(seq_len, num_kv_pairs)` schedule follows the train/test configs in
Hazy Research's `zoology/experiments/mqar_example_configs/original_mqar_configs.py`
extended to the 2048 length where Mamba's state-compression bottleneck is
most pronounced (Arora et al. 2024, Figure 1).

## Metric
The leaderboard metric is **`test_accuracy`** (also emitted as **`score`**):
exact-match accuracy on the next-token prediction at every query position
(positions where the label is not `-100`). The best across all training
epochs is reported (early-best-acc selection, like Zoology's max-acc-per-LR
convention).

## Baselines (variants of the `CustomMixer` slot)
- **transformer** (gold standard) — Vaswani et al. 2017 multi-head causal
  attention via `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention`.
- **lstm** — Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997, the Graves NTM-era recurrent
  baseline.
- **linear_attention** — Katharopoulos et al. ICML 2020
  `phi(x) = elu(x) + 1` linear attention (the non-spiky baseline that BASED
  is designed to beat).
- **based** (SOTA candidate) — Arora et al. ICML 2024
  second-order-Taylor linear attention `k(q,k) = 1 + q^T k + (q^T k)^2/2`
  with the quadratic-view causal scan used at training time in the official
  BASED repo (`zoology/mixers/based.py`, `train_view="quadratic"`).

## Hints
- MQAR fundamentally requires **input-dependent** token mixing: a query
  position has to dynamically attend to the location of its matching key.
  Mixers with data-independent kernels (long convolutions, plain
  state-space models without input gating) tend to plateau well below 100%
  even at the easy `mqar-128` setting.
- The "spikiness" of the kernel matters: high-temperature / low-entropy
  attention isolates a single matching key, whereas uniform-ish kernels
  smear value vectors together. BASED's Taylor-2 kernel is designed to be
  approximately as spiky as softmax while remaining linear-attention
  friendly.
- Be careful with memory at `mqar-2048`: any `[batch, seq, seq]` attention
  matrix uses `~B * T^2 * 4` bytes (~256 MB at `B=16, T=2048`); BASED's
  Taylor-2 quadratic view fits in this budget but a naive `[B, T, D*D]`
  outer-product feature map does not.

tasks.name: Modular Addition Grokking Strategy
tasks.summary: Studies how architecture, optimizer choices, and gradient hooks accelerate grokking on modular addition.
tasks.description_md:
# Synth Modular Addition (Grokking)

## Research Question
On the modular-addition task `y = (a + b) mod p`, can you accelerate or fully
prevent the failure of *grokking* by changing only the **model architecture**,
the **optimizer hyperparameters**, and an **optional per-step gradient hook**,
while keeping every other aspect of the training pipeline fixed?

## Background
Power, Burns, Edwards, Babuschkin, and Misra introduced "grokking" in
"Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets"
(arXiv:2201.02177, 2022). They observed that a small 2-layer transformer trained
on `a + b mod 97` reaches near-100% training accuracy in fewer than 10^3 steps
but only reaches comparable validation accuracy after close to 10^6 steps;
this delayed generalization is dramatically accelerated by AdamW weight decay
(Power 2022, Section 4.1 and Figure 2). Nanda, Chan, Lieberum, Smith, and
Steinhardt later reverse-engineered the algorithm learned by a *one-layer*
transformer on `a + b mod 113` (arXiv:2301.05217, ICLR 2023, Section 3),
showing the model implements a discrete-Fourier circuit. Gromov (arXiv:2301.02679,
2023) further showed that plain two-layer MLPs with a quadratic activation also
grok on the same task. More recently, Lee, Kang, and Choi
(arXiv:2405.20233, 2024) introduced *Grokfast*, gradient filters that
accelerate grokking by roughly 10-20x on modular arithmetic.

In this benchmark, the *dataset construction*, *train/test split*, *loss
function*, *training loop*, and *step budget* are all fixed. Your scientific
freedom is in (a) the **model architecture**, (b) the **optimizer + its
hyperparameters**, and (c) an optional **per-step gradient hook** that runs
between `loss.backward()` and `optimizer.step()` (suitable for techniques
like Grokfast).

## What You Can Modify
Edit the scaffold file
`pytorch-examples/synth_modular_addition/custom_strategy.py` **only** inside
the editable block containing:

1. Any helper `nn.Module` classes you need
2. `build_model(p, config) -> nn.Module`
3. `make_optimizer(model, config) -> torch.optim.Optimizer`
4. `class TrainHook` with `post_grad(self, step)`

The benchmark is evaluated on three primes: `p=59`, `p=97`, `p=113`.

## Fixed Setup
- Task: `y = (a + b) mod p` for `a, b in {0, 1, ..., p-1}`.
- Inputs to the model: `LongTensor` of shape `[B, 2]` with values in `[0, p)`.
- Output of the model: `FloatTensor` of shape `[B, p]` (logits over the `p` classes).
- Loss: cross-entropy.
- Optimization: **full-batch** gradient descent over the training pairs.
- Train/test split: a fixed fraction `train_frac = 0.40` of the `p*p` table,
  with one split per top-level seed.
- Step budget: up to `max_steps = 30000` optimizer steps per run, with early
  stopping if `test_acc >= 0.99` is sustained over 2 consecutive eval windows.
  Runs also stop gracefully at the wall-clock safeguard before the runner's
  30-minute per-seed timeout, recording the latest evaluation metrics as a
  valid non-grokking result if the threshold was not reached.
- Evaluation interval: every 500 steps.

## Interface Notes
- `build_model(p, config)` must return a `torch.nn.Module` whose `forward(x)`
  takes `x: LongTensor[B, 2]` and returns `logits: FloatTensor[B, p]`.
  It must not depend on the train/test split.
- `make_optimizer(model, config)` must return a standard `torch.optim.Optimizer`.
- `TrainHook.__init__(self, model, config)` is called once per run.
- `TrainHook.post_grad(self, step)` is called after `loss.backward()` and
  before `optimizer.step()`; the hook may freely modify `p.grad` of each
  parameter. Returning `None` (the default) means "do nothing".

## Metrics
The leaderboard records, per environment (`p59`, `p97`, `p113`), the mean over
the `num_secrets` runs of:

- `test_accuracy_<env>` -- final held-out accuracy at the last training step
- `score_<env>` -- best held-out accuracy reached at any eval checkpoint
- `mean_steps_to_grok_<env>` -- mean steps at which sustained `test_acc >= 0.99`
  was first reached (set to `max_steps` if the model never groks)
- `grok_rate_<env>` -- fraction of runs that grokked within the step budget
- `best_test_accuracy_<env>` and `train_accuracy_<env>` for diagnostics

The aggregated task score is the geometric mean over the three primes of
`weighted_mean(score_<env>, test_accuracy_<env>)`. Higher is better.

## Baselines (variants of the editable block)
- **default** -- Nanda 2023 reference: 1-layer transformer
  (`d_model=128`, 4 heads, `d_mlp=512`) trained with `AdamW(lr=1e-3, wd=1.0,
  betas=(0.9, 0.98))`, matching the Power 2022 default AdamW hyperparameters.
  Expected to grok on all three primes within the budget.
- **no_wd** -- same architecture and lr but `weight_decay=0`. Expected to fail
  to grok within the budget (Power 2022 Section 4.1: weight decay halves the
  number of samples needed; with no wd the model memorizes and test accuracy
  stays near `1/p`).
- **vanilla_adam** -- same architecture but plain Adam (no decoupled weight
  decay). Should behave similarly to `no_wd`.
- **mlp** -- Gromov 2023 (arXiv:2301.02679) two-layer fully-connected network
  without biases, quadratic activation, one-hot inputs, hidden width 256.
  Demonstrates grokking *without* attention.
- **grokfast** -- Lee 2024 (arXiv:2405.20233) Grokfast-EMA: same baseline
  optimizer with an EMA-of-gradient amplification hook (`alpha=0.98`,
  `lamb=2.0`). Authors report 39,890 -> 2,940 steps (13.57x) for Grokfast-MA
  on modular multiplication mod 97 and about 20x wall-clock reduction in their
  filter experiments.
